research_text:
## Factual research brief

### 1. Governed API and meaning of this finding

`javax.net.ssl.SSLContext` represents a secure-socket protocol implementation. It is a factory for secure socket factories and `SSLEngine` instances, and may be initialized with key managers, trust managers, and a secure-random source. Official API source:  
`https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/javax/net/ssl/SSLContext.html` ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/javax/net/ssl/SSLContext.html))

The reported literal—**“`SSLContext.getDefault()` is forbidden by the expert `SSLContext.crysl`”**—refers to the documented static zero-argument method:

- `SSLContext.getDefault()` returns the JVM’s default `SSLContext`.
- If `SSLContext.setDefault(...)` previously set one, that context is returned; otherwise the first call attempts `SSLContext.getInstance("Default")`, stores the result as the default, and returns it.
- The Java API says this default context is immediately usable and does not require `init(...)`. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/javax/net/ssl/SSLContext.html))

Thus, the finding is about a **call event to `javax.net.ssl.SSLContext.getDefault()`**. It is not, by itself, documentation of enabled protocols, a negotiated TLS version, the certificate-validation behavior of a trust manager, hostname verification, or a TLS handshake result.

The CrySL source declares this call forbidden even though the Java API documents it as valid and immediately usable. That is a rule-policy restriction, not an Oracle API statement that `getDefault()` is invalid or unsafe.

---

### 2. Official API usage and documented remediation

#### Documented `SSLContext` use

The Java API documents these relevant operations:

- `SSLContext.getInstance(protocol)` obtains a new context implementing the requested secure-socket protocol. Without an explicit provider, it searches registered providers and uses the first one that supports the requested protocol. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/javax/net/ssl/SSLContext.html))
- `SSLContext.init(KeyManager[], TrustManager[], SecureRandom)` initializes a context. The API permits either manager array to be `null`, in which case providers are searched for the highest-priority appropriate factory implementation; `random` may also be `null`, in which case a default implementation is used. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/javax/net/ssl/SSLContext.html))
- A context may create an `SSLEngine` or provide socket/server-socket factories. For implementations that require initialization, factory access before `init(...)` can throw `IllegalStateException`. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/javax/net/ssl/SSLContext.html))
- `SSLParameters` is the documented API abstraction for the connection’s allowed protocol list, cipher suites, endpoint-identification algorithm, SNI, and other TLS connection parameters. Its `setProtocols(...)` method sets the protocol array on parameters that can then be applied to a socket or engine. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/javax/net/ssl/SSLParameters.html))

The standard algorithm name `TLS` means “supports some version of TLS” and “may support other SSL/TLS versions.” It does **not** document a fixed enabled or negotiated protocol set. Therefore, neither `SSLContext.getInstance("TLS")` nor the CrySL protocol literal alone establishes what was negotiated on a connection. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/specs/security/standard-names.html))

#### What official sources recommend if `getDefault()` is “used otherwise”

No official Oracle `SSLContext` API source located says that `SSLContext.getDefault()` is improper, insecure, deprecated, or requires a replacement. Accordingly, the official API does **not** provide a “remediation” for use of `getDefault()`.

The only source in scope that prohibits it is the supplied CrySL rule. That rule’s stated compliant ordering is:

- obtain a context through `getInstance(...)`,
- initialize it through `init(km, tm, random)`,
- optionally create an engine,

and it requires a `getInstance` protocol value in exactly `{"TLSv1.2", "TLSv1.3"}` plus the three stated analysis predicates for initialization arguments. Those are CrySL rule conditions, not Java API preconditions. Source:  
`https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/SSLContext.crysl` ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/SSLContext.crysl))

Source limitation: the API documentation permits `null` arguments to `init(...)`, while the CrySL rule requires `generatedKeyManagers[km]`, `generatedTrustManagers[tm]`, and `randomized[random]`. The latter provenance conditions are not documented Java runtime requirements. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/javax/net/ssl/SSLContext.html))

---

### 3. Compatibility and migration documentation

#### Persisted formats

The `SSLContext` API documentation does not specify a persistent serialization format, on-disk configuration format, or data-migration procedure for changing from `getDefault()` to `getInstance(...)`. No such migration path is documented in the cited `SSLContext` API specification.

#### Wire format and negotiated protocol

`SSLContext` is a factory/context API; it is not itself a wire-format API. TLS sessions are created or resumed during the handshake, and `SSLSession.getProtocol()` reports the protocol actually used by a session. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/javax/net/ssl/SSLSession.html))

Changing the context-selection mechanism can nevertheless affect externally visible TLS behavior because:

- `getDefault()` uses the application/JVM default context, which may have been set with `setDefault(...)` or obtained through the `"Default"` algorithm. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/javax/net/ssl/SSLContext.html))
- `getInstance(protocol)` selects a provider implementation for the requested protocol; provider ordering can therefore matter. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/javax/net/ssl/SSLContext.html))
- The JSSE reference guide states that settings for default contexts and default factories can depend on keystore/truststore configuration and provider-specific behavior. It explicitly cautions that some described system-property behavior is reference-implementation behavior and is not guaranteed across future releases or other JSSE implementations. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/17/security/java-secure-socket-extension-jsse-reference-guide.html))

For a change involving `TLSv1.3`, Oracle’s JDK 11 release notes identify protocol-level compatibility considerations relative to TLS 1.2 and earlier, including changed close behavior, different certificate-signature constraints, no DSA certificate support in TLS 1.3, different cipher suites, and different resumption/key-update behavior. The release notes also state that JDK 11 introduced TLS 1.3 and the `TLSv1.3` `SSLContext` algorithm name. ([oracle.com](https://www.oracle.com/java/technologies/javase/11-relnote-issues.html?utm_source=openai))

#### Platform-version support

The documented minimum guarantees differ by Java release:

| Platform documentation | Required/specified `SSLContext` protocol support |
|---|---|
| Java SE 8 API | Requires `TLSv1`; other algorithms depend on the implementation/release. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/javase/8/docs/api/javax/net/ssl/SSLContext.html)) |
| Java SE 11 API | Requires `TLSv1`, `TLSv1.1`, and `TLSv1.2`; Oracle’s JDK 11 release notes separately document implementation of TLS 1.3. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/11/docs/api/java.base/javax/net/ssl/SSLContext.html)) |
| Java SE 17 API | Requires `TLSv1.2`; implementations may support more. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/17/docs/api/java.base/javax/net/ssl/SSLContext.html)) |
| Java SE 25 API | Requires both `TLSv1.2` and `TLSv1.3`. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/javax/net/ssl/SSLContext.html)) |

Therefore, a CrySL requirement accepting `TLSv1.3` should not be treated as portable to every Java runtime merely because the code compiles. The cited specifications and release documentation require confirming the supported JDK/provider combination. No official source reviewed supplies an automatic migration path or compatibility guarantee for a particular application’s peers, provider configuration, trust material, enabled protocol settings, or session behavior.

---

### 4. Exact supplied CrySL rule content and matching scope

Primary CrySL source URL:  
`https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/SSLContext.crysl`

#### Declared governed type

The source begins with:

> `SPEC javax.net.ssl.SSLContext`

So the rule is declared for `javax.net.ssl.SSLContext`. ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/SSLContext.crysl))

#### Exact forbidden matching clause

The verbatim clause is:

> `getDefault() => Get;`

It appears in the `FORBIDDEN` section. ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/SSLContext.crysl))

What the source explicitly states about that clause:

- **Method name:** `getDefault`
- **Parameter list:** empty (`()`), so the declared forbidden event is a zero-argument call.
- **Receiver type:** the rule is declared under `SPEC javax.net.ssl.SSLContext`; the forbidden clause itself does not repeat a receiver type.
- **Following evaluation/action stated by the rule:** the event is forbidden and is mapped to event alias `Get` using `=> Get`.

The source also declares these event signatures:

> `g1: getInstance(protocol);`  
> `g2: getInstance(protocol, _);`  
> `i1: init(km, tm, random);`  
> `se1: eng = createSSLEngine();`  
> `se2: eng = createSSLEngine(_,_);` ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/SSLContext.crysl))

Its stated sequencing and conditions are:

> `Get, Init, Engine?`  
> `protocol in {"TLSv1.2", "TLSv1.3"};`  
> `generatedKeyManagers[km];`  
> `generatedTrustManagers[tm];`  
> `randomized[random];` ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/SSLContext.crysl))

#### Can it match a method that merely shares the name?

**No—not as a generic name-only rule stated by this source.** The source declares its specification type as `javax.net.ssl.SSLContext`; it does not declare a free-standing, all-types `getDefault()` name matcher. The source itself contains no definition of CrySL engine dispatch/type-resolution semantics, so it cannot establish implementation-level details beyond that declared API scope. In particular, from this source alone, it is not possible to prove how a particular analyzer resolves inheritance, static calls, wrappers, or ambiguous symbols; raw diagnostic data and the analyzer/version documentation would be needed for that unresolved implementation question.
